articles.title: Clash in the castle: Medieval Times dinner theater insiders allege animal cruelty, sexual harassment
articles.summary: A former Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament queen alleges sexual harassment, cyberbullying and doxxing in a lawsuit targeting workplace culture.
articles.body: For 43 years, Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament performers across North America have captivated audiences as jousting knights and bejeweled ladies on horseback. But now the company’s own castle is under siege as former employees allege in lawsuits that the company shrouds a culture of animal cruelty, sexual harassment, discrimination, bullying and retaliation for reporting abuse. At the shows, guests dine on what’s billed as a medieval-style feast, as they cheer on armor-clad knights, who participate in a tournament on horseback and battle with swords. The chain established its first location in Kissimmee, Florida, near Orlando, in 1983. The company now employs more than 2,000 at 10 "castles" in the United States and Canada. MEDIEVAL-THEMED LIVE SHOWS DRAW YOUNG WOMEN WHO ARE LOOKING FOR LOVE AND JADED BY MODERN DATING: REPORT The theater’s show champions the "chivalry" of their knights. But some who work alongside those performers say the culture is biased against female cast members. A former "queen" of the castle is now suing the company, alleging a workplace environment "rooted in gender discrimination and sexual harassment." Another whistleblower alleged that she was fired for voicing concerns about animal cruelty. FORMER DISNEY CHANNEL STAR ALLEGES SHE WAS SEXUALLY ABUSED AT 14 AFTER BEING TOLD TO ‘BOND’ WITH EMPLOYEE Royal rivalry A civil lawsuit was filed in June by a former cast member of the Buena Park, California, castle. She alleges a hostile work environment with widespread sexual harassment. Kaitlyn Farrell resigned in February 2024 because of "intolerable" conditions after joining the company as a "queen" five years earlier, according to the lawsuit filed in the Superior Court of California, in Orange County. The "two-tiered workplace culture" treats female cast members as "a lesser class of employee," she said in the lawsuit. Farrell alleges that unwanted sexual advances toward female employees are "normalized" and "gender-based misconduct" and that complaints are "dismissed" with "indifference." While working at Medieval Times, she was asked to be a witness in a workplace harassment investigation for another employee. That made her the "target of open retaliation by the very employee she reported on," her lawsuit alleges. Management stood by and did nothing, she said. On another occasion, according to the lawsuit, a manager ordered someone to "remove stitching" from her costumes, what she calls a "calculated sabotage" that was "maliciously intended to cause wardrobe malfunctions in front of live audiences." After employees unionized at the Buena Park location, and she participated in a strike in February 2023, Farrell said she became the "primary target of an extreme, sexualized cyberbullying and doxxing campaign." Anonymous social media accounts with "obvious indications" of employee or management involvement posted content such as her dating history, sexually derogatory captions and photoshopped images with her face "on the bodies of semi-nude cartoon characters depicted in simulated sexual positions," the lawsuit alleges. DISNEYLAND, ACTORS' UNION CLASH OVER PARENTAL LEAVE, BENEFITS AS UNION NEGOTIATES FIRST CONTRACT The harassment escalated to physical stalking when Medieval Times employees "traveled to Ms. Farrell's secondary workplace" at another theme park "to physically intimidate her while she was working" to entertain guests, the lawsuit alleges. When she made formal complaints about the behavior, an attorney for Medieval Times issued a written letter dismissing the cyberbullying and stalking as "weird allegations." "We look forward to proving these allegations in court," Farrell’s attorney, Charles Ludd Jr., told Fox News Digital. ‘False claims’ Medieval Times did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. But former employee Bill Elliot calls Farrell’s allegations "false claims." Elliot worked at the same Medieval Times location as a knight until leaving after 12 1/2 years in 2015. He had no complaints with the company, he told Fox News Digital in a text message. "The company took care of us," he said. "We had decent pay; full-time hours with overtime … full medical, dental and vision insurance; and 401K." He believes that people making claims against the company are part of "the-rich-need-to-pay-their-fair-share group" and want to cash in, he said. "They have no responsibility in running a company that employs thousands of people and no risk in doing it, but believe they deserve more of the profit," he said. "If it was such a toxic environment and company, they could have immediately removed themselves, but didn't," he said. It was common for female cast members to seek "attention from the knights and [they] did everything to try and get that attention," Elliot said. "Now, because those females didn't get their way or what they wanted, they started making false claims and screaming ‘toxic masculinity’ or any other buzzwords to get attention." Animal-cruelty allegations Farrell’s lawsuit isn’t the first to make concerning claims against the dinner theater company. In her 2019 lawsuit, Bethany Regan tells about how she joined the Buena Park castle in 2013. During her employment, she was treated "less favorably" than male cast members, according to court documents. When she became increasingly concerned about the welfare of the equine performers, she made reports to management, the lawsuit alleges. The head trainer had a "volatile temper" and would whip horses "unnecessarily" until they had "large welts" over their body, according to the lawsuit. Some horses were trained in ways that made them bleed from their mouths and in various places on their bodies, she alleged. Horses were "overworked" and sometimes weren’t allowed to rest until they were dehydrated, according to her complaint. One horse died as a result, she alleged. Regan had been warned that the head horse trainer was a close friend of the owner of the company and that any complaints could result in "retaliation." She brought up her concerns anyway. She also reported "dangerous and unsafe working conditions" for female cast members. After she made formal complaints, the company suspended her for "starting rumors," her lawsuit alleges. Later, her job was terminated. The lawsuit was settled in 2020. The conditions of the settlement were not made public. Regan’s attorney did not respond to a request from Fox News Digital for comment. Horses in the spotlight Yvonne Barteau was principal trainer and director of entertainment operations for six years at Arabian Nights Dinner Attraction. Minutes away from a Florida Medieval Times castle, the horse-themed dinner theater operated from 1988 until 2014. Barteau now runs a horse rescue in Florida called Horses without Humans. She founded the operation after making a documentary about theater horses in the United States. Over the years, she worked with many Medieval Times performers as they moved between dinner theater jobs in the Orlando, Florida, area, she told Fox News Digital. It was common for young performers to get "way too into their role, like they're really medieval warriors," Barteau said. "I think they got too into the identity." That led to men treating women in a "callous" way, she said, "and I think it was not frowned upon the way that it should be. So yeah, certainly back then, I saw it." Dinner theater jobs "seemed to attract people like that. And then sometimes the upper management didn't shut it down like they should have," she said. She met "good people" at Medieval Times. She met others that were not so good, she said. And there’s never an excuse for abusing a horse, she said. "Anybody that works with horses, or works with something that has no voice of its own—children, horses, any animal—you have to be the voice," she said. But "in today’s culture," she said, people with little experience with horses assume that any performance with a horse should be considered cruel. SEND US A TIP And that’s simply wrong, she said. GOT A TIP? "They haven't seen how some horses really do light up, and they do love to be out there performing," she said. "They love the attention." Why would we want somebody else to fall in love with horses?"

articles.title: In 2010, Barbra Streisand disclosed she has built an entire mall under her Malibu estate; the space is equipped with popcorn machine, licorice, vintage costumes, memorabilia, and more
articles.summary: Discover Barbra Streisand's unique underground shopping mall built beneath her Malibu estate. Explore its vintage costumes, antiques, candy shop, and more in this fascinating insight into celebrity life.
articles.body: In 2010, when beloved star Barbra Streisand published her coffee table book, ‘My Passion for Design,' she ended up revealing a major detail about her life. An entire chapter from the book was solely dedicated to her private, subterranean shopping mall built right beneath her Malibu estate. The space had been designed to house decades’ worth of award-winning costumes, rare antiques, and collectibles; this underground village has become an icon of Hollywood lore, inspiring off-Broadway plays and captivating celebrity guests alike. Read ahead to learn the story behind Streisand’s custom-built street, its shops, and why she created it.In 2010, Barbra Streisand revealed that she has her own personal shopping mallUnderneath her 10,000-square-foot Malibu estate, Streisand has built her own special haven in the form of a private shopping mall. The singer was inspired to create the replica 19th-century antique street and display rooms, which house her personal collection of dolls, vintage clothing, and a faux candy/sweet shop—after visiting the Winterthur Museum of American Decorative Arts in Delaware.As per her book, the subterranean promenade was built as a way to keep all of her years' worth of memorabilia, antique collections, costumes, and more in one place. In 2023, while talking to Stephen Colbert on an episode of ‘The Late Show,' the star shared, “It’s a little, tiny mall, if you want to say.” She has also openly talked about the mall and why she made the establishment in her basement.While talking on CBS’ ‘The Today Show’ in 2023, Streisand opened up about her habit of collecting things. She commented, "I love to collect. I love antiques. [As a child] I didn't have a doll, so I put hot water into a hot water bottle, which felt like a real person.”Key features of Barbra Streisand’s private basement mallThere are a lot of features in Streisand’s private mall. These include a candy shop that has been named Baby Rupert’s, which was named after her beloved Coton de Tulear dog, Rupert. It has fully operational candy display cases, vintage dispensers, a popcorn machine, and real licorice and sweets for guests. Along with that, there is a costume and antique shop that houses Streisand’s archival movie wardrobes, stage costumes, vintage lace, and rare textiles. It also has mannequins that are modeling iconic gowns from ‘Funny Girl,' ‘Hello, Dolly!’, and ‘The Way We Were.’She also has her own private doll collection in a shop named Bee's Doll Shop. This space displays her entire collection of antique 19th-century French dolls, porcelain figures, and intricate dollhouses behind glass display windows with working interior lights. Gayle King, the host of ‘The Today Show,’ had heard about Streisand’s collection of hobbies and had joked during the interview, "Wow, Barbra. I think that you've made up for not having a doll when you were a child.”Other than that, there is also a functional nook stocked with wrapping paper, ribbons, cards, and craft supplies where Streisand personally wraps gifts for friends and family. As for the decor and build of the place, it features brick pillars, stone flooring, barn doors, streetlamps, and functioning display windows, with lit interiors to simulate an authentic night stroll down a village street.Many people have gotten a tour of her private mall, which she often treats as part of the guest experience. Some of these people include Oprah Winfrey, Lady Gaga, Ryan Murphy, and Shirley MacLaine.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: El anuncio de la Lotería de Navidad 2026 que emociona: una corazonada, un décimo y una historia de segundas oportunidades
articles.standfirst: Un vídeo enternecedor que te tocará el corazón
articles.summary: Un vídeo enternecedor que te tocará el corazón
articles.body: Cuando falta algo más de un mes para el Sorteo Extraordinario de la Lotería de Navidad, ya se ha presentado el anuncio de la campaña de 2026. El spot, titulado 'Corazonada', sitúa en el centro de su historia la generosidad, la gratitud y las segundas oportunidades a través de una donación de órganos. El protagonista es Edu, un hombre que lleva tiempo esperando una llamada para recibir un trasplante de corazón. Cuando finalmente llega, la operación no solo le permite comenzar una nueva vida, sino que también cambia su forma de mirar el mundo. En un momento del anuncio, Edu tiene una ‘corazonada’ y decide bajarse del autobús varias paradas antes para comprar un décimo. Consigue el último boleto del número que buscaba y, poco después, se encuentra con la hermana del hombre que le donó el corazón. La mujer, que va acompañada de su perro, también pretendía comprar ese mismo número. Edu decide compartir el décimo con ella. “Hace poco, alguien compartió algo muy importante conmigo y me ha dado otra vida”, le explica mientras se lleva una mano al pecho. El gesto conecta el mensaje de la lotería con la historia personal del protagonista. El anuncio se ha rodado en distintas localizaciones de Santander, entre ellas El Sardinero, Cañadío y el Paseo de Pereda. La ciudad cántabra sirve de escenario para una historia que apuesta por las emociones. La presentación llega cuando los décimos llevan a la venta desde principios de julio y queda poco más de un mes para el sorteo, que se celebrará el 22 de diciembre. Este año se repartirán 2.870 millones de euros en premios, 98 millones más que en la edición anterior. El Gordo está dotado con cuatro millones de euros por serie, equivalentes a 400.000 euros por décimo. El segundo premio será de 1.250.000 euros por serie y el tercero, de 500.000. La presentación ha estado marcada desde el primer momento por el recuerdo a las víctimas. El presidente de Loterías, Jesús Huerta, ha comenzado expresando sus condolencias por el accidente y explicando una decisión que ha cambiado el tono habitual de uno de los acontecimientos publicitarios más esperados del año: prescindir de cualquier elemento festivo. "Este año está desprovista de todo elemento festivo por respeto y solidaridad", ha indicado Huerta. También porque la campaña está impregnada de algunos de los valores que considera más representativos de la sociedad española: "La generosidad, la capacidad de compartir y la esperanza".

articles.title: Quote of the day by Katy Perry: ‘If you’re presenting yourself with confidence, you can pull off pretty much anything’
articles.summary: Confidence can often make the difference between holding yourself back and taking a chance on something new.
articles.body: Confidence can often make the difference between holding yourself back and taking a chance on something new. Pop singer Katy Perry once shared a thought that highlights the importance of self-belief and the way we present ourselves to the world. According to Madame Tussauds Singapore, Katy Perry once shared this quote: highlighting the importance of confidence and self-belief.Today's motivational quote of the day, "If you’re presenting yourself with confidence, you can pull off pretty much anything"What does Katy Perry's quote mean?This quote shows us that if you are confident, it can change your attitude and how people see you. You will be more willing to take risks if you know you can do something and are confident with how you are acting. This doesn't mean that confidence can replace talent, practice and hard work, however it can help people to get the best out of their abilities. If you have confidence you won't be as scared to do things like talk in front of people, take on a career opportunity or put yourself in an unknown situation.Why is the quote relevant now?In this competitive world, people often compare their achievements, appearance and progression with others. With social media we are under more pressure to fit certain standards and constantly prove ourselves. This quote is a great reminder that our confidence shouldn't rely on others. It also reminds us that being confident with how we come across doesn't mean we're arrogant. It just means we know our value.Katy Perry's background and rise to fameKaty Perry (born Katheryn Elizabeth Hudson) was born on the 25 th October 1984 in Santa Barbara, California. She was brought up in a very religious household with both of her parents being evangelical pastors. As a result she didn't have much access to mainstream pop/rock music. At the age of 9 she started singing in church and at 13 she learnt how to play the guitar.She started her career in gospel music and released her first album called Katy Hudson in 2001. This wasn't very successful and her record label closed down. From here she shifted to mainstream pop music and moved to Los Angeles.Her journey wasn't easy. She had many failures, failed record deals and financial issues. Eventually she signed with Capitol Records in 2007. In 2008 she released her hit single I Kissed a Girl and became a huge pop star internationally.She went on to release many albums including One of the Boys, Teenage Dream and Prism. Songs such as Hot N Cold, California Gurls, Firework, Roar and Dark Horse helped strengthen her position in the music industry. Over the years she has also been a judge on the singing show American Idol. Katy Perry started her career as a gospel singer and has become one of the most well known names in international pop music. This shows how important it is to be persistent, express yourself and believe in your potential.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Happy Choti Diwali 2026: Share Heartwarming Wishes, Messages, Stunning Images, Thoughtful Quotes and Greetings
articles.summary: Choti Diwali, also called Naraka Chaturdashi, falls on the day right before the main Diwali in most parts of India.
articles.body: Choti Diwali, also called Naraka Chaturdashi, falls on the day right before the main Diwali in most parts of India. It is easy to treat it as a warm-up act, but the day has a character of its own. The idea behind it is simple and hopeful: darkness can be beaten, good can win over evil, and one small flame is enough to give someone courage. Around this time homes begin to glow, kitchens get busy and relatives start calling each other. If you want the right words to go along with all of that, below you will find wishes, quotes and captions you can use, plus the story and traditions behind the festival.Why we celebrate itThe story centres on Narakasura, a powerful demon king who, according to Hindu mythology, made life miserable for gods and ordinary people alike. The more power he gathered, the more arrogant and cruel he became, until peace was out of reach for everyone around him. Lord Krishna, with Satyabhama at his side, finally fought and defeated him. His end brought relief to the people he had oppressed, and the day has been remembered as Naraka Chaturdashi ever since.The lesson goes beyond ritual. Power without compassion causes suffering, and it takes courage to stand up when something is wrong. That is a useful thing to carry into daily life. You can honour the day by dropping an old resentment, admitting a mistake you have been avoiding, or simply treating the people around you with more dignity than you did yesterday.How people observe itPractices differ widely across regions, which is part of what makes the festival so rich. In many homes, family members wake up before sunrise for Abhyanga Snan, a ritual oil bath linked with purification and shedding negativity. Lamps are then lit at entrances, windows, balconies and the prayer corner, and their warm glow is a reminder that light always beats the dark.Decorating is a big part of the fun. Rangoli patterns appear at doorsteps, marigolds and flowers are strung up, and colourful torans hang over the entrance. Meanwhile the kitchen turns out sweets and savoury snacks, and families start welcoming guests ahead of the main celebration. In Bengal the day overlaps with Kali Puja, so the worship of Goddess Kali takes centre stage there. No two places celebrate in exactly the same way, and that variety is the point.20 wishes to sendMay these little diyas bring you big reasons to smile and blessings that last all year. Happy Choti Diwali! Every lamp you light is a reminder that hope never disappears, even in the darkest hour. Wishing you a beautiful Naraka Chaturdashi.May your home be full of laughter, your heart full of gratitude and your days full of moments that matter.Let the victory of good over evil nudge you toward kindness, courage and honesty, today and every day.Wishing you a festival of homemade sweets, familiar faces, long conversations and memories worth keeping.May peace settle into your home, along with the strength to let go of whatever has been holding you back.As every diya glows, may it bring a little more understanding, compassion and warmth to the people around you.May your hard work pay off, your dreams find their direction and your loved ones always have something to celebrate.I hope your happiness this Choti Diwali comes from simple things, like a shared meal or an honest chat.May the days ahead open new doors, bring unexpected opportunities and leave you deeply content.Goodness doesn’t have to be loud to make a difference. Happy Naraka Chaturdashi!May your celebration be as colourful as rangoli, as warm as a diya and as sweet as the best mithai.Wishing you the courage to get through hard days and the wisdom to notice the good already around you.Let every diya you light stand for a promise: to be kind, to forgive freely and to stay grateful.Here’s to your family’s good health, togetherness, prosperity and plenty of moments worth remembering.May Choti Diwali bring a fresh beginning, brighter possibilities and your favourite people close by.Share a little more, worry a little less, and find joy in making someone else’s day special.Wishing you a celebration that brings generations together through stories, traditions, laughter and love.May the light of Naraka Chaturdashi guide you toward better choices, stronger relationships and a calmer life.Happy Choti Diwali! articles.title: Martha Stewart sits down with Craig Melvin to address halloween costume controversy
articles.summary: Martha Stewart apologized on TODAY following her controversial Halloween costume that appeared to depict a homeless person and said Craig Melvin was not at fault for her wearing the outfit that sparked a backlash.
articles.body: Martha Stewart apologized on TODAY following her controversial Halloween costume that appeared to depict a homeless person and said Craig Melvin was not at fault for her wearing the outfit that sparked a backlash. The 85-year-old lifestyle guru has been facing criticism since she posted a now-deleted photo of her looking disheveled while holding a clipboard that read, “I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!” for Halloween, per NBC News. During her appearance on TODAY Nov. 6, Stewart addressed the controversy and how Craig got roped into it. “I made a mistake,” Stewart said. “I was stupid, what else can I say? I am so sorry, and I hope that my followers and my fans and the rest of America forgives me for doing something that was not meant in any way to be a bad thing.” Craig then asked Stewart about reports that said she claimed she wore the last-minute costume because he spilled chocolate on her sweater during their TODAY Halloween special segment on Oct. 30, where Craig was dressed as rapper Snoop Dogg. “I didn’t have a costume because you had spilled some chocolate on my white sweater, and I don’t blame you at all,” she told Craig. “It was a joke that I said I blamed you. It was stupid.” Stewart said she was giving a talk and made a joke that Craig had spilled chocolate on her so she couldn’t wear that costume and pivoted to the other one instead. “Of course, they picked up on that because you’re you,” Stewart said. “But I did apologize for spilling the chocolate,” Craig said. “We moved on.” “And it wasn’t your fault,” Stewart said. She also shared feedback she received from her family. “Tone-deaf, or whatever I was. According to my grandson, I was tone-deaf,” she said. “He saw the picture first because I sent it to him and I said, ‘What do you think?’ ‘Tone-deaf,’ he said. It was just stupid, and I apologize because I was not making fun of anybody or making light of the great problems that face our country.” Stewart, who will return to TODAY next week for the annual All-Star Thanksgiving segment, shared what she learned from the controversy. “Pay closer attention to social issues,” she said. “Be aware. I’m aware of all those social issues, as you can imagine, and I care desperately about all the problems facing us.” For her Halloween costume, Stewart wore torn clothing and covered her face in makeup to resemble dirt. Her Instagram post with a picture of the costume doubled as an ad for her candle collection on QVC. “My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!” she captioned the since-deleted post. After some criticized the costume for being “out of touch” and “dystopian,” according to NBC News, Stewart reacted to the negative responses in a statement. “I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” she said in a statement to NBC News on Nov. 1. Homelessness, she wrote, “continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic.” At the end of her statement, Stewart added, “I am committed to continuing to make a difference.” Stewart then penned a second statement that she shared on her Instagram page on Nov. 1, as well. “It’s hard to admit when you’ve really screwed up. My earlier statement didn’t go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry,” she wrote. The post has since been deleted.

articles.title: Stranger Things is getting a live-action spinoff called Other Worlds
articles.summary: Netflix announced a prequel series called Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure that will start streaming in 2028.
articles.body: Netflix isn’t done with Hawkins, Indiana just yet. The streamer just announced a live-action spinoff of Stranger Things which is expected to debut in 2028. It’s called Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure. There aren’t a lot of details, but the show will be going back in time quite a bit. According to Netflix, Other Worlds is “a prequel set in the 1950s, before Stranger Things and before the stage play Stranger Things: The First Shadow.“ Franchise creators the Duffer brothers are back on board, and Stranger Things veteran Kate Trefry will serve as showrunner. British director Joe Wright is set to helm the first three episodes. In a statement, the Duffers described the series as “Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting.“ It’s been clear that Netflix has been looking for ways to keep its most impactful series alive ever since Stranger Things wrapped up with its final season last year. So far that has included the animated spinoff Tales From ‘85, but a live-action series appears to show a much bigger effort behind expanding the franchise.

articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'Godzilla Minus Zero' and 'Wild Horse Nine' in theaters, rent or buy 'Resident Evil,' stream 'Carolina Caroline' on Netflix
articles.summary: Our critic's take on the latest film releases — from another Godzilla sequel to "The Cat in the Hat" to Sylvester Stallone and Jimmy Stewart biopics.
articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to notable new movies opening or becoming available each Friday.

It's a busy week in theaters! Godzilla Minus Zero, the highly anticipated sequel to Japan's Godzilla Minus One, debuts nationwide in the U.S. alongside Wild Horse Nine, an Oscar player starring Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich ( read our interview with the stars here ). I Play Rocky also debuts in select theaters ahead of a wider release in a few weeks.

If you'd prefer a movie night at home, you can rent or buy Zach Cregger's smash-hit Resident Evil, or the Chris Hansen/ To Catch a Predator movie Primetime.

Over on streaming services you're likely already paying for, Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner will charm you in Carolina Caroline, now on Netflix, and Super Troopers 3 debuts on Hulu.

The buzziest release: Godzilla Minus Zero

Why you should see it: Godzilla Minus One, a Japanese-made Godzilla flick, became an unexpected global smash hit following its 2023 debut. Its melodramatic story of a Japanese fighter pilot brought an almost arthouse sensibility to what would otherwise have been a blockbuster monster-movie spectacle.

The sequel Godzilla Minus Zero doubles down on these elements. While the human melodrama unfortunately overwhelms this time, the movie still delivers the jaw-dropping action and destruction where it matters in big, exciting ways.

Minus Zero sports an R rating, the first in the franchise's 72-year history, and there's a new level of brutality to the violence here that really stresses the " Godzilla movies are metaphors about nuclear war and the atomic bomb" of it all. The movie is very much about the trauma a population faces following a war, which manifests in several ways.

Two years have passed since the events of Minus One , and Japan has faced agonizing struggles to recover and finally reclaim its daily life. Just as humanity has managed to cling to a hard-won peace, a new threat strikes, crushing hope in an instant.

The movie opens with the introduction of a new monster — other critics have revealed this, but I found it best left unspoiled — and that first set piece rocks. This new monster becomes the centerpiece of the film's best sequence, an aerial dogfight between kaiju and humans in airplanes.

Whenever the movie isn't in blockbuster action-sequence mode, however, it slows down to the point where you'll likely be checking your watch. There's a new complication in the mix involving a survivor of a past Godzilla attack, and I'm not sure the movie properly explores it. There's another character who lost his wife and kid to a Godzilla attack, though, which leads to a memorable NYC-set dream sequence. I found that imagery unforgettable and its ideas about revenge potent.

Godzilla Minus Zero may not feature quite enough Godzilla for some of the lizard's most diehard fans, but its exploration of big ideas similar to those explored in Chris Nolan's Best Picture-winning Oppenheimer does still render it far more impactful than your average giant monster movie.

What other critics are saying : It's getting good reviews, mostly, but they all have caveats like mine. The AV Club's Matt Schimkowitz writes that it's "not a bad movie, and it's an above-average Godzilla film. But it's also a different type of throwback, one that recalls the days when you wouldn't be roared at for checking your watch during the human scenes." The Associated Press's Jake Coyle was even less enthusiastic, writing, "If every Godzilla film is building toward its finale, Minus Zero doesn't stick the landing."

How to watch: Godzilla Minus Zero is now playing in theaters nationwide .

The expected Oscar darling: Wild Horse Nine

Why you should see it: What Wild Horse Nine lacks in originality it more than makes up for with its nasty sense of humor and soulful reflection of a man facing the end of his life and attempting to find meaning in it.

Martin McDonagh, the beloved Irish filmmaker whose previous efforts have earned several Oscar nominations, from Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri to The Banshees of Inisherin, returns to familiar territory here. The premise itself sounds identical to the setup for his debut, 2008's In Bruges, a personal favorite of mine that stars Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson as hitmen lying low after a tough job.

Wild Horse Nine follows CIA agents Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell) as they are dispatched to Easter Island shortly before the coup in Chile in 1973. As the longtime partners wrestle with their dark pasts and present conspiracies, Chris's newfound bond with a pair of rebellious students threatens to send everyone's trip on this remote paradise sideways.

By setting the movie against the backdrop of very real historical events, McDonagh adds a layer of social commentary and critique about American interventionism abroad. At the same time, the movie is laugh-out-loud hysterical throughout, full of the sardonic wit and cracking dialogue for which McDonagh is known. Most of the laughs come from the bickering between Rockwell and Malkovich, both of whom are Oscar-worthy. Malkovich's lack of discretion, such as when he openly discusses staging military coups to anyone within earshot, is particularly funny. There's a running gag involving Steve Buscemi's character that has a terrific and very silly payoff.

Wild Horse Nine might not bring a litany of new ideas to the table, but it engages with old ones in ways that are both entertaining and thought-provoking.

What other critics are saying : It's well-reviewed! Amy Nicholson at the Los Angeles Times writes, "Only classic screwball comedians have delivered dialogue as blithely as Malkovich does here, with zingers that float off unburdened by the heaviness of the real world." Kristy Puchko at Mashable , meanwhile, says that the film is "deepened by its repetition," citing connections to its stars' previous roles.

How to watch: Wild Horse Nine is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why you should see it: Anthony Ippolito's performance as Sylvester Stallone is so uncanny, there are a few shots in the film where your mind actually tricks you into believing you're watching archival footage of Stallone making Rocky. Stallone's manner of speaking and entire persona are so distinctive that a sustained impersonation shouldn't work, but Ippolito sells it so well, it's not a problem at all.

Rocky is one of the greatest and most rousing crowd-pleasing underdog stories of all time, so making a movie about it is kind of a cheat code already . But what really makes it sing is that Stallone's journey of getting Rocky — and himself — on the big screen is an underdog story of its own.

The movie starts with Stallone calling himself Mike, despite his real name being Sylvester. He's an unknown actor with an unshakable belief that he wasn't just meant to write Rocky — he was meant to be Rocky Balboa. Told "no" at every turn, Stallone bets everything on himself, holding the line on playing the lead against seemingly impossible odds.

Much of the movie's drive comes from the negotiations with the studio, which is doing everything in its power to make Rocky without Stallone in the lead role, while the actor remains indignant, saying he won't let them. Everyone thinks he's a madman, but it's that belief in himself and his refusal to give up on his dream that make the movie so affecting and effective. There's a poetic poignancy here, even if the movie gets a little repetitive with the back-and-forth of "this guy won't play Rocky" and "this guy must play Rocky."

Ultimately, Ippolito sells the hell out of it. It's charming!

What other critics are saying : They like it! David Rooney at The Hollywood Reporter writes, "The element that holds the movie together is Ippolito, who nails the garbled, rumbling diction, hangdog expression and hulking physicality of Stallone while never losing sight of his insecurities at this unproven point in his career." Variety's Owen Gleiberman writes, "The pleasure of I Play Rocky is that it understands the karmic way in which the story of Rocky — the underdog who triumphs against all odds — was echoed in the saga of how Stallone got the movie off the ground."

How to watch: I Play Rocky is now playing in select theaters before expanding on Nov. 20.

Cat in the Hat : There's "doing too much," and then there's this. This new adaptation of the 1957 Dr. Seuss classic adds so much lore and so many complications that it barely resembles the very simple story upon which it's based. The film immediately sets up a Monsters, Inc. -like world in which Seussian creatures like the Cat in the Hat are assigned to bored children to help them have a nice day. He ends up being assigned to siblings Gabby and Sebastian as they adjust to life in a new town. Known for pushing boundaries, the Cat in the Hat is an agent of chaos who must prove himself or risk losing his magical hat forever. It's incredibly busy and borrows from several kids' flicks, never settling on a single energy. Get tickets .

Jimmy : KJ Apa, Archie on the TV series Riverdale, is excellent as Jimmy Stewart in this movie, which tells the story of an actor's life that didn't get as much attention as his movie stardom. It's far more about his time in the U.S. military and how, despite the Hollywood system begging him to use his celebrity to get out of serving, Stewart felt compelled to fight for his country anyway, movie career be damned. I do wish the movie spent more time on the Hollywood stuff, but there's always room for a sequel, I suppose. Get tickets .

Why you should watch it: There have already been seven Resident Evil movies — six of them in a more action-oriented series starring Milla Jovovich, four of which were directed by her husband, Paul W.S. Anderson, plus an unrelated "reboot" in 2021 called Welcome to Raccoon City that went for more of a John Carpenter vibe and was more of an attempt to truly "adapt" the games. There's also a Netflix TV show version that ran for a single season in 2022. Countless other works in the horror genre have unofficially cribbed from the Resident Evil games over the years. It's an incredibly influential series.

And yet, Zach Cregger, hot off his Oscar-winning original horror film Weapons, is the first filmmaker to truly feel like he's adapting the experience of playing the games, arguably the scariest survival-horror ones ever made, rather than simply incorporating story and plot elements to explain the outbreak of infected people. In Cregger's hands, Resident Evil is pure crowd-pleasing popcorn cinema, best experienced in a packed movie theater with dozens of other people reacting loudly to the madness.

The premise couldn't be simpler — and the runtime a brisk 90 minutes — as we follow a medical courier named Bryan (Austin Abrams, proving himself to be the Bruce Campbell for a new generation) who unwittingly finds himself fighting for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in a swirl of chaos. Fans of the video games will recognize various Easter eggs and nods to game mechanics, including the importance of conserving ammo and checking every last drawer for more of it.

But you don't need to be familiar with the games at all to enjoy the movie, which is an efficient horror set-piece machine that just keeps putting Abrams in increasingly concerning situations. I can't stress enough how much this is a one-man show anchored by Abrams, and he crushes it. He's in every scene, earning tons of laughs simply by reacting as a normal person would in this situation; he's a true audience-surrogate character, ushering us through the chaos. His comedic timing, paired with Cregger's assured camerawork and editing, is a match made in genre-movie heaven.

I didn't expect it to be so heavily inspired by genre classics like The Thing and Evil Dead. In fact, it's a better Evil Dead movie than the last several movies with " Evil Dead " in the title, nailing the horror-comedy tone that only Sam Raimi and a few others can pull off with aplomb. Cregger has a ton of fun with the various monstrous forms that the infected take here, from fusing multiple humans together to crafting his own horror take on a big, scary guy like Dune 's Baron Harkonnen. Resident Evil movies have thus far treated the zombies as pretty traditional movie zombies; Cregger's version gets at the attempt to create the next stage of human evolution.

Zach Cregger's Resident Evil may not feature characters that gaming fans recognize, but it's spiritually more in line with the games than any of the ones that do. Adaptation stuff aside, it's also just a heart-pounding, adrenaline-fueled roller-coaster ride of a movie that has no grander ambitions than getting a rise out of the audience over and over again. It's a blast, and this time, you can't pause it, put your controller down and walk away when things get too intense.

What other critics are saying: The previous seven installments were panned by critics every time; the opposite is true here, as Cregger's take sports a near-perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Independent's Clarisse Loughrey writes, "It feels thoroughly like a film by Zach Cregger ... proving that subtle, psychological work isn't always the superior horror when you have a filmmaker who can deliver a jump scare shock with this much elegant panache." Jesse Hassenger at the Guardian writes, " Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag."

How to watch: Resident Evil is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Why you should watch it: Primetime is the first narrative feature from documentarian Lance Oppenheim (the codirector of Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything ). It functions best as a companion piece to last year's must-see documentary, David Osit's Predators, which I reviewed here and called a thought-provoking, bleakly hilarious look at our nation's unhealthy obsession with true crime as entertainment.

That description works just as well as a summation of Primetime ; both films are about the early-2000s NBC series To Catch a Predator, a spinoff of Dateline hosted by Chris Hansen, and the exploitative nature of the show despite its "good for society" intention of catching, publicly shaming, and arresting real-life pedophiles.

Primetime follows Hansen, as played by Robert Pattinson, in a disturbing, mannered, over-the-top caricature of a performance that works extremely well in this context. Hansen sets out to make television history by turning his undercover investigation into one of the decade's most controversial cultural phenomena, not to mention a hit show that rivaled big-budget entertainment like Lost in the ratings.

That's just one element of the plot, though, as we also follow one of the actors who plays the decoy children used as bait; Skyler Gisondo is terrific as the naive up-and-coming actor seeking his big break and finding it on To Catch a Predator. We also spend a lot of time with the show's producer, played by Merritt Wever, who seems to revel in the lurid excitement of it all despite the potential dangers.

Hansen himself, as depicted here, is both self-aggrandizing and self-loathing, and eventually becomes troubled by the impact of his work . "What would have happened if I wasn't here?" starts as something he tells a guy ensnared in the show and morphs into an acknowledgment of culpability. When a man recognizes him on an airplane and thanks him for his work, adding, "I don't know how you do it, I'd kill those guys with my bare hands," Hansen responds, "I think what I do is worse."

It really can't be stressed enough how unbelievably good Pattinson is — there's a multifacetedness to the performance that really gets at Hansen's contradictions, especially in the way he presents himself on television vs. how he acts in private. It's a performance of a character who's constantly performing; Pattinson makes you laugh and makes you uneasy, often in the same sequence.

Primetime is clever in how it gets at its messaging; there's a sequence that unfolds as if Hansen is grooming Gisondo's character to take advantage of him, much like the titular predators would with a child they target. But the documentary Predators threads the needle way more effectively on the idea of the inherent exploitation of "if it bleeds, it leads"-style salaciousness as entertainment, whereas the movie's subtle gestures at the same ideas just don't hit as hard.

The section of the documentary that focuses on YouTubers who have taken it upon themselves to mete out vigilante justice in the name of the program contains some of the most enlightening and upsetting material, and none of it makes it into this movie. And that's fine — they have different narrative goals — but Predators just feels like it tells a fuller story. Primetime's limited scope, however, allows it to go all in on Hansen in a way that's nightmarish and unsettling.

The movie is also a darkly hilarious time capsule of the Bush-era "you're either with us or with the bad guys" mentality, connecting the period's broader cultural and political landscape to the vigilante justice craze. Gisondo's arc is also one of the darker A Star Is Born- style narratives about what it takes to make it in the industry. The film is quite beautifully made, featuring various era-appropriate video formats whose grit adds to its intentionally grimy quality, as if you're watching a found VHS tape from some nightmare world.

Primetime is an incredibly well-acted movie full of memorable performances — I haven't stopped repeating Wever's frantic line of "Puca shells? No puca shells?" — that gets at the incongruity between sensationalist exploitation and need-to-know news. It's a movie about the kind of person you need to be to succeed in an unethical world, and how people like that make the world more unethical as they succeed. It may tread familiar ground, but it does so bombastically enough to entertain and is thought-provoking all the same. It brings up a lot of uncomfortable questions and contradictions that don't have easy answers.

What other critics are saying: It's getting rave reviews, but is not without its detractors. Rolling Stone's David Fear writes, " Primetime recounts how this show didn't create a sense of collective bloodlust; it just rode a wave that was already there. Then it tells us we're free to go, knowing what awaits us right outside the front door." Amy Nicholson at the Los Angeles Times , however, found it to be too much, writing, "There's not a single shot of a healthy human being in the movie, only wraiths filmed in sickly shades of pink, red and blue."

How to watch: Primetime is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother: Mahershala Ali is terrific in this movie about a devoutly religious hit man struggling to balance work, faith and fatherhood. After his wife dies, he embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children as he confronts the forces that are closing in around him. John Cho also stands out as the scenery-chewing villain. Rent or buy .

The History of Concrete: John Wilson of HBO's beloved docuseries How To With John Wilson makes his feature debut with this hilarious, idiosyncratic and totally on-brand documentary that's ostensibly about, well, the history of concrete. But in the process, it's really about the human experience. It's not as pretentious and lofty as that sounds — in fact, it's as hysterical as it is insightful and purely fascinating. Wilson's fans are in for a treat, as it plays pretty much identically to his series, though it does gesture toward some deeper, perhaps darker, revelations about society. (You may find yourself wondering, "What do Chef Boyardee, or a guy who hands out free booze at liquor stores, have to do with the idea here?") But in a uniquely John Wilsonian fashion, it all feels quite revelatory and makes perfect sense by the end. It works great as an introduction to his sensibilities as a documentarian for newcomers and functions just as well as an expansion of his television work for those familiar. Rent or buy .

Sense and Sensibility : A new take on Jane Austen's iconic novel, this is a charming, witty and deeply relatable story of love and sisterhood starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles . Rent or buy .

📺 Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

Why you should see it: Remember back in the '90s when it seemed like every indie movie was about lovers on the run? Carolina Caroline is such a strong entry into this particular canon that you'll be hoping it spurs another wave of 'em.

In this sexy crime romance, a young woman (Samara Weaving), desperate to leave her small town, runs away with a charming con man (Kyle Gallner) and embarks on a crime-and-passion-filled journey through the Southeast to find her estranged mother. It feels indebted to Badlands and Natural Born Killers as much as to Bonnie and Clyde. T here's also the added element of a con and the act of teaching someone how to pull it off, reminiscent of Will Smith and Margot Robbie's Focus, to name a fairly recent example.

Carolina Caroline may be the best showcase of Weaving, who has thus far largely played scream queens in horror movies but rarely gets to show her true range. I've repeatedly praised her work in dozens of extremely bad genre movies, with my usual refrain being that she is always the best thing about them. She's generally far better than the movies she appears in; Carolina Caroline may be the first one that feels worthy of her talent.

That's not to shortchange Gallner, who is every bit as good as Weaving here. He's another actor who's been quietly racking up credits for decades — his first was 2001's Wet Hot American Summer — and found himself doing great work in genre fare, often in character-actor-type smaller roles. He's wonderful in a lead role here, equal parts charming and menacing.

Carolina Caroline works because its central romance does. It's electric stuff, and you feel it. The pitch-perfect country-western soundtrack helps with that too. It's an engaging, engrossing crime thriller that's full of tension. Don't miss this indie gem!

What other critics are saying: They like it! Vikram Murthi at the AV Club writes, "Both Weaving and Gallner excel playing distressed criminals who feel the heat on their tail, but the way that distress curdles into shared heartbreak and grief as they slowly reach clarity draws serious blood." Variety's Guy Lodge correctly points out that the two leads should be bigger stars, writing, "Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner, two fine actors rarely granted the glow that comes with a proper star vehicle, positively bask in it here; together, they give a potentially standard film an active heart rate."

How to watch: Carolina Caroline is now streaming on Netflix .

Why you should see it: There was a 17-year gap between the original Super Troopers and its crowdfunded sequel, which is so forgettable that I barely remember it, other than as a massive disappointment.

Fans of the Broken Lizard comedy troupe didn't have to wait that long for another bite at the apple, though, as another sequel is here. Luckily, it's a major improvement on 2018's Super Troopers 2. When Farva's over-the-top Indian engagement to Thorny's sister spirals into chaos, the Super Troopers must navigate Thorny's schemes to break up the relationship, all while trying to bring down a pernicious new drug ring.

It goes for broad, cheap laughs and only sometimes works; every lazy reference to now-iconic jokes from the original is eye-roll-worthy. But there's a lot that did make me laugh in here, including some out-of-left-field Star Wars- inspired silliness in the final act. I found that it got better as it went along, and really won me over by the end.

What other critics are saying: Most were not as kind as I was. TheWrap's William Bibbiani writes, "If all you want is to see these lovable goofballs again, you'd be better served watching the first two Super Troopers movies and reliving their good old days. Those films are still mostly funny and the new days aren't so good." Jesse Hassenger at the AV Club , however, was more on board: "As with its predecessors, ramshackle high spirits carry Super Troopers 3 through its less inspired patches, and toward the group's more charming comic tastes."

How to watch: Super Troopers 3 is now streaming on Hulu .

The Uprising : This perfectly serviceable but rather dull historical action film is overtly political and doesn't have to tie itself in knots to make connections between the 1381 Peasants' Revolt in England and how wealth and power function today. It's not subtle about it; the rebelling commoners are at one point referred to as "deplorables." Andrew Garfield plays the leader of a ferocious rebellion against the tyranny of King Richard II, forming an army of the people to face the king's might in a fight for justice. The most interesting thing about this movie is, unfortunately, extratextual, as the U.S. marketing pivoted late in the game to calling it The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood. It also emphasized that the film was "set against the true events of the uprising that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood," even as the non-U.S. marketing departments insisted that it was not, in fact, about Robin Hood. I can confirm, dear reader, that the movie does, in fact, pivot to a stealth origin story for Robin Hood eventually, much like it unfolded in the press: at the absolute last minute! It's far more compelling as a movie about the Peasants' Revolt than as a Robin Hood picture, and that's without getting into the muddying of timelines for those who care about historical accuracy. Now streaming on Peacock .

Motor City : A compilation mixtape in search of a movie, Motor City is an almost entirely wordless action movie that assumes audiences will be happy with bare-minimum plotting as long as a song they enjoy is playing. In 1970s Detroit, John Miller ( Alan Ritchson ) falls for a local gangster's girl and lands in prison for a crime he didn't commit. With his life ruined, Miller plots revenge against the man who took his girl away. There's a scene early on that just plays the entirety of Fleetwood Mac's "The Chain," a four-and-a-half-minute song, over a slow-motion action scene. It's so incredibly labored that the audience I saw it with was laughing at the movie, not with it. Every scene is unnecessarily stretched out in similar ways, and you feel every second. It's gimmicky BS, frankly, that flattens the material into the most generic version of itself possible in an attempt to be different. Now streaming on AMC+ .

Making Marie Antoinette : This lovely and deeply personal film is far more than a behind-the-scenes documentary about the making of Sofia Coppola's 2006 film Marie Antoinette . What makes it so special is that it's compiled from incredible on-set footage shot by Coppola's late mother, Eleanor. The Coppola matriarch's notes and observations from the time come alive via narration from actor Diane Lane, providing rare insight into the famous family and their artistic process. You can actually feel Eleanor's pride in her daughter beaming off the screen, and it's infectious. You also get to see Coppola leading a massive production as a young, relatively inexperienced female filmmaker, with sequences that showcase her struggle to realize her artistic vision amid various challenges, including male crew members who often think they know better. It's fascinating, insightful and just an incredibly moving work of art about a mother's admiration for her daughter. Now streaming on Mubi .

That's all for this week! We'll see you next Friday.

articles.title: Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku
articles.summary: A few months after DOJ investigators were probing the deal, Fox just completed its $22B acquisition of the streaming giant Roku.
articles.body:
Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.

Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.

“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”

For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.

Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.

The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.
